title: Options: The Right, Not the Obligation

cards.headline: A contract, not a share.
cards.body: An option is a contract. It gives you the **right** — but never the obligation — to buy or sell a stock at a set price before a set date. You pay for that right up front.

cards.headline: Two types: calls and puts.
cards.body: A **call** is the right to **buy** a stock at a fixed price; a **put** is the right to **sell** one. A call gains if the price rises far enough, a put if it falls.

cards.headline: Every contract has four parts.
cards.body: The **type** (call or put), the **strike** (the fixed price), the **expiration** (the deadline), and the **premium** (what the contract costs). Change any one and you have a different contract.

cards.title: A call buyer's payoff
cards.caption: Buy a $100 call for **$5**. Below $100 you lose only the $5 premium. Above **$105** — strike plus premium — every extra dollar is profit.

cards.body: Every option has two sides. One pays for a right; the other sells it and takes on a duty.

cards.prompt: You buy a $100 call for $5. At expiration the stock is $103. Are you ahead?

options.label: No — I need $105 to break even

cards.explanation: The stock cleared the **strike**, but not by enough to cover the $5 premium. Break-even is strike plus premium: $105. At $103 you recover $3 of the $5 you paid.

cards.headline: Sellers can be assigned.
cards.body: If you **sell** an option and it finishes in the money, you can be **assigned** — forced to honour it. A call seller must deliver shares; a put seller must buy them, at the strike.
The most an option **buyer** can lose is the [[1]] they paid for the contract.
cards.explanation: A buyer's loss is capped at what they paid. If the option expires worthless, the premium is gone — but never more than that.

cards.headline: Small bets, big swings.
cards.body: One contract usually controls **100 shares**, so a little money moves a lot of exposure. That cuts both ways: options can multiply a gain, expire at zero, and — for sellers — carry very large losses.

cards.summary: An option is a paid right to buy or sell at a set price by a set date — powerful, and easy to lose in full.
bullets: Calls are the right to buy; puts, the right to sell.
Buyers risk only the premium; sellers can owe far more.
Break-even is the strike plus the premium you paid.

cards.insight: An option is not a share. It is a bet on a price by a deadline, and if the deadline wins, the bet expires at zero.

sources.title: Investor Bulletin: An Introduction to Options
sources.publisher: U.S. SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy
